notes: Aberfan flood nuisance appeal; common enemy rule, foreseeability, and ECHR arguments are fully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Aberfan flood nuisance and the common enemy rule
key_facts: Thirty-two Aberfan residents' homes were flooded in October 1998 when the river Taff overtopped its banks after Grove Fields had been raised by ten to twelve feet with colliery spoil.
The infilling of Grove Fields, carried out in the 1970s by the council and National Coal Board, was accepted at trial as a material cause of the flooding.
Royce J dismissed the nuisance claims principally because the common enemy rule applied and because flood damage was not reasonably foreseeable when the works were done.
The appeal considered whether the common enemy rule should be modified under Article 8 ECHR and Article 1 of the First Protocol.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a High Court trial dismissing private nuisance claims arising from the October 1998 Aberfan flood.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the common enemy rule applied and the causal link between the infilling and interior flood damage was not reasonably foreseeable.
enrichment.ratio: The common enemy rule permits a landowner to protect his land from flood waters even if water is diverted onto a neighbour's land, subject to limits against interfering with an alveus or exporting floodwater already on one's land; reasonable foreseeability of damage is a separate and necessary condition for nuisance liability.
legal_issues: Whether the common enemy rule applied to inland properties not abutting the riverbank
Whether the rule should be modified under the Human Rights Act 1998
Whether flood damage to the appellants' homes was reasonably foreseeable when Grove Fields was infilled
Whether the council's landlord status affected liability

notes: Probate revocation on failed execution and knowledge and approval; witness evidence is detailed and outcome clear.

enrichment.short_title: Revocation of probate for invalidly executed solicitor's will
key_facts: Richard Sherrington, a wealthy solicitor, executed a will on 7 September 2001 leaving his entire estate to his second wife Yvonne, excluding his three children from his first marriage.
The will was drafted in haste by Yvonne's daughter Dr Walker, who had never drafted a will before, and was witnessed by Mrs Butt and Mr Thakkar without their knowing it was a will.
Richard Sherrington died in a car crash on 30 October 2001; probate was granted to Yvonne in May 2002 on an estate valued at about £2.8m for probate but closer to £10m in real terms.
The children challenged probate on due execution and knowledge and approval grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery claim for revocation of a grant of probate to the deceased's widow.
enrichment.outcome: Probate revoked; the defendant failed to prove due execution and knowledge and approval of the will.
enrichment.ratio: Strict compliance with section 9 of the Wills Act 1837 is required and attesting witnesses must intend to verify the testator's signature; where a beneficiary instrumental in preparing a will leaves everything to herself despite a tempestuous marriage and devoted children, suspicion is not dispelled without proof of knowledge and approval.
legal_issues: Whether the will was duly executed under section 9 of the Wills Act 1837
Whether attesting witnesses intended to verify the testator's signature
Whether the deceased knew and approved the contents of the will
Whether the will reflected the deceased's known wishes

notes: Criminal Proceedings Order under section 42; extensive chronology of vexatious private prosecutions supports indefinite order.

enrichment.short_title: Indefinite Criminal Proceedings Order against vexatious litigant
key_facts: Mr Ebert was already subject to a Civil Proceedings Order made on 7 July 2000 after extensive High Court litigation culminating in a bankruptcy order.
Since June 2000 he had laid informations in multiple magistrates' courts alleging criminal conduct against twelve defendants including bankers, solicitors, judges, and court officials.
District judges repeatedly refused or stayed proceedings, finding the allegations ill-founded, malicious, and an abuse of the criminal process.
The Attorney General applied for a Criminal Proceedings Order of indefinite duration under section 42 of the Supreme Court Act 1981.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's application for a Criminal Proceedings Order under section 42 of the Supreme Court Act 1981.
enrichment.outcome: Indefinite Criminal Proceedings Order granted; Mr Ebert may not lay informations or apply to prefer a bill of indictment without leave of the High Court.
enrichment.ratio: A Criminal Proceedings Order under section 42 may be made where a person habitually and persistently institutes vexatious prosecutions without reasonable ground; 'vexatious' means little or no legal basis, disproportionate harassment, and abuse of process, and an indefinite order may be proportionate where lesser measures would be ineffective.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Ebert had habitually and persistently instituted vexatious prosecutions
The meaning of 'vexatious' under section 42
Whether an indefinite Criminal Proceedings Order was proportionate
Whether Mr Ebert received a fair hearing
linked_authorities: Attorney General v Barker [2000] 1 FLR 759
Attorney General v Jones [1990] 1 WLR 859
Attorney General v Matthews [2001] EWCA Civ 254

notes: Important CPR 19.5 point on LTA 1954 s29(3) time limit; Court of Appeal allowed substitution after four-month period.

enrichment.short_title: Substituting landlord after LTA 1954 section 29(3) deadline
key_facts: Tenants of Mansted House school premises applied for a new tenancy under Part II of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954 within the four-month period prescribed by section 29(3).
The claim form named the executors of the late Mrs Stedman as defendants, but the freehold had been transferred to Mrs Purcell on 23 April 2003 before the claim was issued.
After the four-month period expired, the tenants applied to substitute Mrs Purcell as the competent landlord.
The deputy district judge held CPR 19.5 gave no power to substitute a party after the section 29(3) deadline.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court refusal to substitute the correct landlord after expiry of the section 29(3) limitation period.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; substitution permitted under CPR 19.5 where the wrong landlord was named by genuine mistake and the same solicitors acted for both landlords.
enrichment.ratio: CPR 19.5(1)(c) applies to statutory limitation periods that do not prohibit a change of parties, including section 29(3) of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954; substitution is permitted after expiry where the limitation period was current when proceedings started and the new party was named in mistake for the correct landlord.
legal_issues: Whether CPR 19.5 applies to the section 29(3) four-month limitation period
Whether the court could substitute the correct landlord after that period expired
Whether CPR 19.2 or CPR 3.10 provided an alternative route
Whether the mistake fell within CPR 19.5(3)(a)

notes: Rent Act succession and assured tenancy status; brother's letter construed as surrender not assignment.

enrichment.short_title: Rent Act succession letter held not to assign assured tenancy
key_facts: Mrs Macnicol claimed an assured tenancy by succession after her mother, a statutory tenant of 2B Ravenscroft Avenue, died in February 1999.
Both Mrs Macnicol and her brother Mr Khawaja claimed succession rights; the judge found she had agreed in March 1999 that he would be the claimant.
On 4 July 2000 Mr Khawaja wrote to the landlord giving up all rights to the tenancy so his sister could remain, after the landlord refused a joint tenancy.
Mrs Macnicol later accepted an assured shorthold tenancy in October 2001, which the landlord then terminated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court possession order based on assured shorthold tenancy status.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the July 2000 letter was a surrender of succession rights, not an assignment of an existing assured tenancy.
enrichment.ratio: Where rival claimants to a Rent Act succession have not yet been determined, there is no existing assured tenancy capable of assignment; a letter to the landlord giving up rights in favour of a sibling should be construed as surrender of a succession claim, not assignment in breach of section 15 of the Housing Act 1988.
legal_issues: Whether Mrs Macnicol was an assured tenant or assured shorthold tenant
Whether the 4 July 2000 letter effected an assignment of an assured periodic tenancy
Whether Mrs Macnicol qualified for succession under the Rent Act 1977
Whether an assignment required a deed

confidence.notes: Core construction issue and statutory framework are clearly resolved, though some factual findings on residence were not appealed.

notes: Planning s288 challenge; inspector's decision quashed for failing to assess actual flood risk despite upholding PPG 25 sequential test.

enrichment.short_title: Planning appeal quashed over tidal flood risk assessment
key_facts: Thomas Bates sought planning permission for 124 dwellings at Hall Road, Heybridge, Essex, adjacent to the Blackwater Estuary tidal flood plain.
A previous appeal decision in the claimant's favour was quashed; a reopened inquiry addressed only tidal flooding under PPG 25.
The Environment Agency accepted proposed flood management measures provided 1 in 200 year protection, but the inspector dismissed the appeal on sequential test and high flood risk grounds.
The site was a Zone 3(a) developed area on PPG 25 flood plain maps, with lower-risk housing sites available elsewhere in the district.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to an inspector's decision dismissing a planning appeal after a reopened inquiry on flood risk.
enrichment.outcome: Decision quashed on grounds 2, 3 and partially 5; the inspector correctly applied the PPG 25 sequential test but failed properly to assess actual flood risk and comparative site vulnerability.
enrichment.ratio: The PPG 25 sequential test is based on flood zone categories from indicative maps without regard to defences until no reasonable lower-risk options remain; once lower-risk sites exist, defended status does not save a higher-zone site, but actual flood protection must still be weighed as a material consideration in the overall balance.
legal_issues: Correct interpretation of the PPG 25 sequential test and Table 1
Whether flood defences should be considered at the zoning stage of the sequential test
Whether the inspector failed to assess actual flood risk given accepted 1 in 200 year defences
Whether comparative flood risk to Jacob's Farm site was properly evaluated

confidence.notes: Mixed outcome on grounds is clearly explained; PPG 25 interpretation upheld but factual flood risk assessment criticised.

notes: Magistrates' adjournment quashed after prolonged delay and unexplained failure to warn prosecution witnesses.

enrichment.short_title: Quashing magistrates' adjournment for unwarned witnesses
key_facts: Mr Irwin was charged with making twelve hoax calls to a fire brigade and faced repeated adjournments over nearly two years before trial.
Eleven of twelve charges were dismissed as out of time; a single charge proceeded through multiple pre-trial reviews and vacated trial dates.
On 13 February 2004 prosecution witnesses failed to attend because they had not been warned despite the file indicating warnings were required.
The magistrates reluctantly granted a further prosecution adjournment without explanation; the defendant was in poor health.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a magistrates' court decision granting a prosecution adjournment on the trial date.
enrichment.outcome: Adjournment quashed and the remaining information dismissed; application for judicial review allowed.
enrichment.ratio: Magistrates may adjourn under section 10 of the Magistrates' Courts Act 1980, but an adjournment requires a reason and explanation; where prosecution witnesses were not warned without explanation after a protracted history of delay, fairness no longer permitted further adjournment.
legal_issues: Whether magistrates properly exercised discretion to adjourn the trial
Whether refusal to adjourn would have caused substantial unfairness
Whether the prosecution's failure to warn witnesses justified stopping the case
Application of R v Hereford Magistrates' Court, ex parte Rowlands
linked_authorities: R v Hereford Magistrates' Court, ex parte Rowlands [1998] QB 110
R v Aberdare Justices, ex parte Director of Public Prosecutions [1990] COD 324

notes: Supplementary costs judgment after partial success on arbitration interest challenge; unqualified foreign lawyer point decisive.

enrichment.short_title: Arbitration costs after unqualified solicitor bar
key_facts: Westland Helicopters challenged arbitrator Mr Tackaberry's award of interest from 1985 on a quantum meruit retainer claim by Mr Al-Hejailan.
Westland partially succeeded: interest before January 1995 was set aside under sections 67 and 68 of the Arbitration Act 1996.
Mr Al-Hejailan's solicitor Mr Thoms, an American attorney in a Saudi law firm, had acted throughout the arbitrations but was not entitled to act as solicitor in English court proceedings.
Section 25(1) of the Solicitors Act 1974 precluded recovery of costs for work done by unqualified persons acting as solicitors.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Supplementary costs judgment following a successful partial challenge to an ICC arbitration award.
enrichment.outcome: Westland recovered 70% of its costs of both applications; Mr Al-Hejailan could recover no costs because his lawyers were unqualified to act as solicitors in England.
enrichment.ratio: Where an unqualified person acts as solicitor in High Court proceedings, section 25(1) of the Solicitors Act 1974 precludes recovery of all costs normally included in a solicitor's bill, including counsel's fees, leaving nothing to set off against an opponent's costs order.
legal_issues: Appropriate costs apportionment after partial success on arbitration challenge applications
Whether Mr Thoms could act as solicitor in English court proceedings
Effect of section 25(1) of the Solicitors Act 1974 on recovery of counsel's fees
Whether any set-off of costs was available to Mr Al-Hejailan

notes: Article 8 appeal from IAT in Kosovo asylum case; Shala distinguished and proportionality restored.

enrichment.short_title: Article 8 family life claim refused for Kosovo asylum seeker
key_facts: Mr Alihajdaraj, an ethnic Albanian from Kosovo, arrived in the UK in October 1998 and claimed asylum; his cousin Driton Beqiri was granted indefinite leave to remain in June 1999.
The Secretary of State refused asylum in December 2000 and maintained that refusal in September 2002; an Article 8 claim was raised only at the adjudicator hearing in March 2003.
The adjudicator found family life with extended relatives including weekly contact with his cousin and held removal disproportionate, citing immigration delay.
The IAT allowed the Secretary of State's appeal on proportionality; the claimant appealed to the Court of Appeal relying on Shala.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision restoring a removal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; removal to Kosovo was a proportionate interference with Article 8 family life.
enrichment.ratio: Shala turns on its facts and does not assist where delay before June 1999 was shorter, family ties are tenuous, and no independent right to remain exists; maintaining effective immigration control carries substantial weight and removal of a healthy young man with distant cousin contact is proportionate.
legal_issues: Whether Article 8 family life existed between the claimant and his cousin and extended family
Whether removal was a disproportionate interference with Article 8.2 rights
Application of Shala v Secretary of State for the Home Department
Whether the IAT was entitled to overturn the adjudicator's proportionality assessment

Janjanin v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] EWCA Civ 448

notes: Trust taxation on stock dividends under ss249 and 686; Special Commissioners' decision upheld on construction.

enrichment.short_title: Trust taxation on stock dividends under sections 249 and 686
key_facts: Trustees of the Robin Settlement held 35 ordinary shares in a company and elected to receive 70,000 bonus 1p shares worth over £15m in lieu of a £700 cash dividend.
Section 249 deemed the trustees to receive income equal to the grossed-up market value of the bonus shares, with notional tax at the 10% Schedule F ordinary rate.
The Revenue assessed additional tax at the 25% Schedule F trust rate under section 686, producing liability of about £2.5m.
Under the settlement terms the bonus shares were capital receipts in the trustees' hands, not income for trust law purposes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Special Commissioners upholding additional Schedule F trust rate tax on stock dividends received by discretionary trust trustees.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; section 686 applied and the trustees were liable to tax at the Schedule F trust rate on the deemed income.
enrichment.ratio: Where bonus shares are issued to trustees of an accumulation or discretionary settlement within section 249(6), the deemed income in section 249(6)(b) is income for trust law purposes and falls within section 686(2)(a) as income to be accumulated or payable at the trustees' discretion, attracting the Schedule F trust rate.
legal_issues: Whether 'income' in section 249(6)(b) means income under the Taxes Act or under trust law
Whether section 686 applies where bonus shares are capital receipts in the trustees' hands
Interaction of sections 249, 686 and 687 on stock dividend treatment
Whether the trustees' construction would produce an anomalous tax advantage
linked_authorities: Chetwode v Inland Revenue Commissioners [1977] 1 WLR 248
Liversedge v Anderson [1942] AC 206
